title: The Silver Era Hercules: Steve Reeves (Legends of the Past)
summary: Episode two of NH's Legends of the Past series profiles Steve Reeves as the model natural bodybuilder in body and mindset. He covers Reeves' fatherless childhood, training in secret during WWII despite malaria, his Greek-proportion ideals, three full-body sessions a week, carb-heavy whole-food diet and anti-steroid stance. He also covers Reeves' Hercules film career and his view that fitness should enhance life, not dominate it.
claims: Modern natural lifters need role models from the past who did things properly
Steve Reeves, born 1926, lost his father before age one; his mother made him wear a brace that poked him whenever he slouched, giving him perfect posture
Reeves started lifting after losing an arm-wrestling match to a smaller boy who lifted weights
NH started working on himself after losing an arm-wrestling match to a small girl
As a teen Reeves had good lat and core development but skinny arms, shoulders and legs, which is normal for teenagers
In WWII Reeves caught malaria four times and lost 30 lb, yet rebuilt by secretly lifting a 210 lb barbell under his bed every day
Reeves' stats: 6'1", 210-225 lb, 18.5-19 in arms, 52 in chest, 29 in waist, 26 in thighs, 18.5 in calves
Reeves was around 10% body fat, not shredded, just carrying a lot of lean muscle
Reeves followed Greek proportions (arms equal to neck and calves, arms not bigger than the head) and stopped training calves until his arms caught up
NH disagrees with strict Greek proportions as a personal aesthetic but grants they're objectively defensible
Reeves used visualization, picturing his muscle fibers working and growing in an almost hypnotic focus
Mentally checking out and going through the motions in training may leave a piece missing; focus on the muscle
Reeves trained full body three times a week with plenty of rest, crushing every muscle each session
In full-body sessions train legs last; opening with squats and deadlifts leaves no energy for presses
Reeves' order: shoulders and chest, lats and biceps, triceps, quads, hamstrings, calves, lower back, abs, neck
Reeves trained abs and neck seriously with isolation, as every bodybuilder should
Reeves used antagonist supersets to save time and do more work
Reeves chased an extra rep every session and loved slow negatives
Reeves power-walked briskly over long distances about four times a week; NH sees it as a good way to stay healthy
Good natural nutrition advice should center on whole foods
Reeves ate about 60% carbs, 20% protein and 20% fat; NH uses a similar carb-heavy split, though fat versus carb preference is individual
Reeves ate most of his carbs the day before training to be full of glycogen; NH does the same
'No pain, no gain, no brain, no gain': suffering without intelligence gives no results
Reeves said a man without enough natural hormones for a hard muscular body should take up ping pong rather than use steroids
Bodybuilders who use steroids aren't really bodybuilders; natural bodybuilders are the real ones
Directors asked Reeves to lose up to 20 lb of muscle to look average; he refused, seeking a balanced physique and life
Building your body is building your life; people who ignore their body live imbalanced lives
Ancient warriors looked athletic like Reeves, not like pro bodybuilders; even NH is a bit too bulky for that role
Reeves dislocated his shoulder doing his own chariot stunt and kept filming, which wrecked the shoulder
Reeves died at 74 from a blood clot after surgery, not from disease
A good male power fantasy started from a relatable place: skinny, poor posture, losing to a smaller kid
Fitness should enhance the rest of your life, not consume it; Reeves had many interests outside bodybuilding
exercises: upper body first, legs last, antagonist supersets, slow negatives
save energy for presses and fit in more work
